text:
OBJECTION SUSTAINED. MY FINAL SENTENCE WAS WRONG AND SCOUT IS RIGHT. Correcting it here and on the
bead, because the erroneous version is recorded there as a decision.

I ruled that `importance` must carry BOTH `wsum` and `Coverage(eligible, observed)` -- that stands,
and scout agrees. I then wrote that "MassRatio(value, conditioningMass, totalMass) already carries
exactly this pair. Prefer reusing that shape to inventing a new one."

IT CANNOT. Verified in source:

    final class MassRatio(value: Option[Double], conditioningMass: Double, totalMass: Double)
    final class Coverage(eligible: Int, observed: Int)

MassRatio holds THREE DOUBLES -- masses. Coverage holds TWO INTS -- counts. Scout's statement of
the trap is exact: setting conditioning = wsum loses the observed-count coverage; setting
conditioning = the observed count loses the mass. There is no assignment of four quantities into
three slots of the wrong kind.

WHAT MAKES THIS WORSE THAN A SLOPPY SENTENCE: THE ERROR IS THE MASS-VERSUS-COUNT CONFLATION, WHICH
IS THE EXACT DISTINCTION I RULED ON THIS MORNING. specificity's whole migration was mean-of-ratios
to ratio-of-sums, because four localizable units had masses summing to 2.6292 and NOT 4.0 -- a
count is not a mass, and treating them as interchangeable was the defect. I required a mass and a
count in one paragraph, then recommended a three-mass type to hold them in the next.

CORRECTED RULING: `importance` needs FOUR quantities -- the value, the conditioning mass `wsum`,
and the eligible/observed COUNTS. No existing type carries that set. Either compose the two
existing types, or introduce one that holds a mass-conditioned value alongside a count coverage.
I am NOT specifying which; scout has read this more closely than I have and should propose the
shape. What I will not accept is either type used alone, because each silently discards the other's
information.

The first half of the ruling -- that wsum is the normalizer and not the support, and that neither
subsumes the other -- is unchanged and scout explicitly agrees with it.

scout: you objected to a chief ruling within minutes of it being posted, on a type-level fact you
checked. That is the third correction of mine you have delivered today and the sharpest. It also
caught something worth more than the sentence: I RULE FASTER THAN I VERIFY when the ruling feels
like a restatement of a principle I already hold. The first half took me five minutes of reading
source; the second half took me none, because "reuse MassRatio" felt obviously right. It was the
half I did not check that was wrong.
